metadata.title: wurtylex/LeanECC (Lean blueprint)

extraction_notes.note: Hamming distance $\Delta(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})$, relative distance $\delta(\cdot,\cdot)$ and the $q$-ary entropy $H_q$ are used but never defined in the source, so no definition nodes exist for them.
The proof of the linear-code Gilbert-Varshamov bound is the placeholder 'TODO'; kept as a proof node with zero steps.
definition or lemma: the environments assert existence of the matrix (the content of LP6/LP8) before naming it; kept as definition, with inferred edges from LP6/LP8.
The blueprint formalizes textbook material ('conventions of Essential Coding Theory'); uncited standard definitions and lemmas are marked external per Hard rule 3, their proofs paper.

metadata.extraction_comment: Vol_q's arguments appear in both orders (Vol_q(n,r) and Vol_q(r,n)) in the source; both are taken as the same volume.

nodes.name: Code
nodes.statement: A code $C$ of block length $n$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a subset of $\alpha^{n}$. Typically, we will use $q$ to denote the alphabet size $|\Sigma|$.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
differentia: of block length $n$ over an alphabet $\alpha$
nodes.label: def:Code

nodes.name: Alphabet Size
nodes.statement: The alphabet size is $q := \lvert\alpha\rvert$, the cardinality of the finite alphabet $\alpha$.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
nodes.label: def:q

nodes.name: Dimension
nodes.statement: The dimension $k$ of a code $C$ is \[ k := \log_{q}(\lvert C\rvert), \] where $q$ is the alphabet size and $\lvert C\rvert$ is the number of codewords.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
nodes.label: def:dim

nodes.name: Rate
nodes.statement: The rate $R$ of a code $C$ is \[ R := \frac{k}{n}. \] where $k$ is the dimension and block length of $n$.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
nodes.label: def:rate

nodes.name: Minimum Distance
nodes.statement: Let $C \subseteq \Sigma^{n}$. The minimum distance of $C$, denoted $\Delta(C)$, is defined to be \[\Delta(C) = \min_{\mathbf{c_{1}} \neq \mathbf{c_{2}} \in C} \Delta(\mathbf{c_{1}}, \mathbf{c_{2}}).\]
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
nodes.label: def:MinDim

nodes.name: Relative Minimum Distance
nodes.statement: Let $C \subseteq \Sigma^{n}$. The minimum distance of $C$, denoted $\delta(C)$, is defined to be \[\delta(C) = \min_{\mathbf{c_{1}} \neq \mathbf{c_{2}} \in C} \delta(\mathbf{c_{1}}, \mathbf{c_{2}}).\]
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
nodes.label: def:RelMinDim

nodes.name: Hamming Ball
nodes.statement: For any vector $\mathbf{x} \in [q]^{n}$, \[B(\mathbf{x},e) = \{\mathbf{y} \in [q]^{n}\mid \Delta(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) \leq e\}.\]
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
nodes.label: def:HammingBall

nodes.name: Volume
nodes.statement: \[V_{q}(n,r) = \sum^{r}_{i = 0} \binom{n}{i}(q-1)^{i}\] where $r$ is the radius.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
nodes.statement_short: Volume of a Hamming ball: $V_q(n,r)=\sum_{i\le r}\binom{n}{i}(q-1)^i$.
nodes.label: def:Vol

nodes.name: Maximal With Respect to Inclusion
nodes.statement: Let $C\subseteq \Sigma^{n}$ with minimum distance denoted $\Delta(C)$. $C$ is defined to be maximal with respect to inclusion if: \[\forall C' \subseteq \Sigma^{n}, C\subseteq C', \Delta(C) = \Delta(C') \implies C'\subseteq C\]
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
nodes.statement_short: A code is maximal if no superset code has the same minimum distance.
nodes.label: def:maximalWrtInclusion

nodes.name: Dimension is at most the block length
nodes.statement: For every code $C$ of block length $n$, we have $k \leq n$.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
nodes.label: lem:dim_le_n

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: Note that $C \subseteq \alpha^{n}$, we have $\lvert C\rvert \le \lvert\alpha\rvert^{n} = q^{n}$, thus $k = \log_{q}\lvert C\rvert \le \log_{q} q^{n} = n$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|C|\le q^n$ and take $\log_q$.

nodes.name: Rate is at most one
nodes.statement: For every code $C$, we have $R \leq 1$.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
nodes.label: lem:rate_le_one

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:dim_le_n}, $k \leq n$, and $n \ge 0$. Therefore $R = k/n \leq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Divide $k\le n$ by $n$.

nodes.name: Sphere cardinality
nodes.statement: For any $\mathbf{x} \in [q]^n$ and integer $i \geq 0$, \[\bigl|\{\mathbf{y} \in [q]^n \mid \Delta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = i\}\bigr| = \binom{n}{i}(q-1)^i.\]
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
nodes.statement_short: The Hamming sphere of radius $i$ in $[q]^n$ has $\binom{n}{i}(q-1)^i$ points.
nodes.label: lemma:SphereCard

nodes.name: Proof of Sphere cardinality
nodes.statement:
Write $S_i = \{\mathbf{y} \in [q]^n \mid \Delta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = i\}$ for the sphere, and for a word $\mathbf{y} \in [q]^n$ let \[ T(\mathbf{y}) = \{j \in [n] \mid y_j 
eq x_j\} \] be its set of disagreement coordinates. By the definition of Hamming distance, $\Delta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = |\{j \in [n] \mid x_j 
eq y_j\}| = |T(\mathbf{y})|$, so membership $\mathbf{y} \in S_i$ is the same as the condition $|T(\mathbf{y})| = i$. We construct an explicit bijection. Let $\mathcal{P}_i$ be the set of pairs $(T, g)$ in which $T \subseteq [n]$ has $|T| = i$ and $g : T 	o [q]$ satisfies $g(j) 
eq x_j$ for every $j \in T$. Define the forward map \[ \Phi : S_i 	o \mathcal{P}_i, \qquad \Phi(\mathbf{y}) =  igl(T(\mathbf{y}),\ (y_j)_{j \in T(\mathbf{y})} igr); \] this is well defined because $|T(\mathbf{y})| = i$ by the paragraph above, and $y_j 
eq x_j$ for each $j \in T(\mathbf{y})$ by the definition of $T(\mathbf{y})$. Define the reverse map \[ \Psi : \mathcal{P}_i 	o S_i, \qquad \Psi(T, g) = \mathbf{y}, \quad	ext{where } y_j =  egin{cases} g(j) & 	ext{if } j \in T, \ x_j & 	ext{if } j 
otin T. \end{cases} \] Its image lies in $S_i$: the word $\mathbf{y} = \Psi(T, g)$ has $y_j 
eq x_j$ exactly on $T$ (on $T$ since $g(j) 
eq x_j$, and off $T$ since $y_j = x_j$), so $T(\mathbf{y}) = T$ and therefore $|T(\mathbf{y})| = |T| = i$. The two maps are mutually inverse:  egin{itemize} \item $\Psi(\Phi(\mathbf{y})) = \mathbf{y}$: on $T(\mathbf{y})$ the reconstructed word takes the value $y_j$, and off $T(\mathbf{y})$ it takes the value $x_j$, which equals $y_j$ because $j 
otin T(\mathbf{y})$ means exactly that $y_j = x_j$. \item $\Phi(\Psi(T, g)) = (T, g)$: we showed $T(\Psi(T, g)) = T$, and on $T$ the values kept by $\Phi$ are the $g(j)$. \end{itemize} Therefore, $|S_i| = |\mathcal{P}_i|$. It remains to count $\mathcal{P}_i$. Grouping the pairs by their first coordinate $T$, \[ |\mathcal{P}_i| = \sum_{\substack{T \subseteq [n] \ |T| = i}}  igl|\{\, g : T 	o [q] \mid g(j) 
eq x_j 	ext{ for all } j \in T \,\} igr|. \] For a fixed $T$, specifying such a $g$ means choosing, independently for each $j \in T$, one of the $q - 1$ values in $[q] \setminus \{x_j\}$; there are thus $(q-1)^{|T|} = (q-1)^i$ such functions. As the number of $i$-element subsets of $[n]$ is $ inom{n}{i}$, \[ |S_i| = |\mathcal{P}_i| = \sum_{\substack{T \subseteq [n] \ |T| = i}} (q-1)^i =  inom{n}{i}(q-1)^i. \]
nodes.statement_short: Explicit bijection between the sphere and pairs (support set, nonmatching values), then count the pairs.

nodes.name: Disagreement set
nodes.statement: Write $S_i = \{\mathbf{y} \in [q]^n \mid \Delta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = i\}$ for the sphere, and for a word $\mathbf{y} \in [q]^n$ let \[ T(\mathbf{y}) = \{j \in [n] \mid y_j \neq x_j\} \] be its set of disagreement coordinates. By the definition of Hamming distance, $\Delta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = |\{j \in [n] \mid x_j \neq y_j\}| = |T(\mathbf{y})|$, so membership $\mathbf{y} \in S_i$ is the same as the condition $|T(\mathbf{y})| = i$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce sphere $S_i$ and disagreement set $T(\mathbf{y})$; membership is $|T|=i$.

nodes.name: Forward map
nodes.statement: We construct an explicit bijection. Let $\mathcal{P}_i$ be the set of pairs $(T, g)$ in which $T \subseteq [n]$ has $|T| = i$ and $g : T \to [q]$ satisfies $g(j) \neq x_j$ for every $j \in T$. Define the forward map \[ \Phi : S_i \to \mathcal{P}_i, \qquad \Phi(\mathbf{y}) = \bigl(T(\mathbf{y}),\ (y_j)_{j \in T(\mathbf{y})}\bigr); \] this is well defined because $|T(\mathbf{y})| = i$ by the paragraph above, and $y_j \neq x_j$ for each $j \in T(\mathbf{y})$ by the definition of $T(\mathbf{y})$.
nodes.statement_short: Define pairs $\mathcal{P}_i$ and the forward map $\Phi$; check well-defined.

nodes.name: Reverse map
nodes.statement:
Define the reverse map \[ \Psi : \mathcal{P}_i 	o S_i, \qquad \Psi(T, g) = \mathbf{y}, \quad	ext{where } y_j =  egin{cases} g(j) & 	ext{if } j \in T, \ x_j & 	ext{if } j 
otin T. \end{cases} \] Its image lies in $S_i$: the word $\mathbf{y} = \Psi(T, g)$ has $y_j 
eq x_j$ exactly on $T$ (on $T$ since $g(j) 
eq x_j$, and off $T$ since $y_j = x_j$), so $T(\mathbf{y}) = T$ and therefore $|T(\mathbf{y})| = |T| = i$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the reverse map $\Psi$ and check its image lies in $S_i$.

nodes.name: Mutual inverses
nodes.statement: The two maps are mutually inverse: \begin{itemize} \item $\Psi(\Phi(\mathbf{y})) = \mathbf{y}$: on $T(\mathbf{y})$ the reconstructed word takes the value $y_j$, and off $T(\mathbf{y})$ it takes the value $x_j$, which equals $y_j$ because $j \notin T(\mathbf{y})$ means exactly that $y_j = x_j$. \item $\Phi(\Psi(T, g)) = (T, g)$: we showed $T(\Psi(T, g)) = T$, and on $T$ the values kept by $\Phi$ are the $g(j)$. \end{itemize} Therefore, $|S_i| = |\mathcal{P}_i|$.
nodes.statement_short: Check $\Phi,\Psi$ are inverse, so $|S_i|=|\mathcal{P}_i|$.

nodes.name: Psi after Phi
nodes.statement: $\Psi(\Phi(\mathbf{y})) = \mathbf{y}$: on $T(\mathbf{y})$ the reconstructed word takes the value $y_j$, and off $T(\mathbf{y})$ it takes the value $x_j$, which equals $y_j$ because $j \notin T(\mathbf{y})$ means exactly that $y_j = x_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Verify $\Psi\circ\Phi$ is the identity.

nodes.name: Phi after Psi
nodes.statement: $\Phi(\Psi(T, g)) = (T, g)$: we showed $T(\Psi(T, g)) = T$, and on $T$ the values kept by $\Phi$ are the $g(j)$.
nodes.statement_short: Verify $\Phi\circ\Psi$ is the identity.

nodes.name: Reduction to counting
nodes.statement: It remains to count $\mathcal{P}_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to counting $\mathcal{P}_i$.

nodes.name: Group by support
nodes.statement: Grouping the pairs by their first coordinate $T$, \[ |\mathcal{P}_i| = \sum_{\substack{T \subseteq [n] \\ |T| = i}} \bigl|\{\, g : T \to [q] \mid g(j) \neq x_j \text{ for all } j \in T \,\}\bigr|. \]
nodes.statement_short: Write $|\mathcal{P}_i|$ as a sum over supports $T$.

nodes.name: Count value functions
nodes.statement: For a fixed $T$, specifying such a $g$ means choosing, independently for each $j \in T$, one of the $q - 1$ values in $[q] \setminus \{x_j\}$; there are thus $(q-1)^{|T|} = (q-1)^i$ such functions.
nodes.statement_short: Each support admits $(q-1)^i$ value functions.

nodes.name: Conclude count
nodes.statement: As the number of $i$-element subsets of $[n]$ is $\binom{n}{i}$, \[ |S_i| = |\mathcal{P}_i| = \sum_{\substack{T \subseteq [n] \\ |T| = i}} (q-1)^i = \binom{n}{i}(q-1)^i. \]
nodes.statement_short: Sum over the $\binom{n}{i}$ supports.

nodes.name: Ball cardinality equals volume
nodes.statement: For any $\mathbf{x} \in [q]^n$ and $r \geq 0$, \[|B(\mathbf{x}, r)| = \Vol_q(n, r).\]
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
nodes.label: lemma:BallCard

nodes.name: Proof of Ball cardinality
nodes.statement: For each integer $0 \leq i \leq r$ let $S_i = \{\mathbf{y} \in [q]^n \mid \Delta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = i\}$ be the sphere of radius $i$ about $\mathbf{x}$. The $S_i$ are pairwise disjoint: if $\mathbf{y} \in S_i \cap S_j$ then $i = \Delta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = j$, so distinct indices give disjoint spheres, as a word has a single Hamming distance to $\mathbf{x}$. The $S_i$ also cover the ball. By the definition of the Hamming ball, $\mathbf{y} \in B(\mathbf{x}, r)$ means $\Delta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) \leq r$. Since $\Delta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})$ is a nonnegative integer, this holds iff $\Delta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = i$ for exactly one $i$ with $0 \leq i \leq r$, i.e. iff $\mathbf{y} \in S_i$ for some such $i$. Therefore, \[ B(\mathbf{x}, r) = \bigsqcup_{i=0}^{r} S_i, \] a disjoint union by the previous paragraph. Finally, we compute the cardinalities. Because the union is disjoint, its cardinality is the sum of the cardinalities of the parts, and each part is counted by Lemma~\ref{lemma:SphereCard}: \[ |B(\mathbf{x}, r)| = \sum_{i=0}^{r} |S_i| = \sum_{i=0}^{r} \binom{n}{i}(q-1)^i. \] The right-hand side is exactly $\Vol_q(n, r)$ by the definition of the volume, so $|B(\mathbf{x}, r)| = \Vol_q(n, r)$.
nodes.statement_short: Partition the ball into disjoint spheres and sum the sphere cardinalities.

nodes.name: Spheres
nodes.statement: For each integer $0 \leq i \leq r$ let $S_i = \{\mathbf{y} \in [q]^n \mid \Delta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = i\}$ be the sphere of radius $i$ about $\mathbf{x}$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce spheres $S_i$, $0\le i\le r$.

nodes.name: Disjointness
nodes.statement: The $S_i$ are pairwise disjoint: if $\mathbf{y} \in S_i \cap S_j$ then $i = \Delta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = j$, so distinct indices give disjoint spheres, as a word has a single Hamming distance to $\mathbf{x}$.
nodes.statement_short: Spheres of distinct radii are disjoint.

nodes.name: Covering
nodes.statement: The $S_i$ also cover the ball. By the definition of the Hamming ball, $\mathbf{y} \in B(\mathbf{x}, r)$ means $\Delta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) \leq r$. Since $\Delta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})$ is a nonnegative integer, this holds iff $\Delta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = i$ for exactly one $i$ with $0 \leq i \leq r$, i.e. iff $\mathbf{y} \in S_i$ for some such $i$. Therefore, \[ B(\mathbf{x}, r) = \bigsqcup_{i=0}^{r} S_i, \] a disjoint union by the previous paragraph.
nodes.statement_short: The ball is the disjoint union of the spheres.

nodes.name: Sum cardinalities
nodes.statement: Finally, we compute the cardinalities. Because the union is disjoint, its cardinality is the sum of the cardinalities of the parts, and each part is counted by Lemma~\ref{lemma:SphereCard}: \[ |B(\mathbf{x}, r)| = \sum_{i=0}^{r} |S_i| = \sum_{i=0}^{r} \binom{n}{i}(q-1)^i. \] The right-hand side is exactly $\Vol_q(n, r)$ by the definition of the volume, so $|B(\mathbf{x}, r)| = \Vol_q(n, r)$.
nodes.statement_short: Sum sphere sizes via Sphere cardinality and match the volume.

nodes.name: Volume entropy bound
nodes.statement: Let $q \geq 2$ and $n \geq 1$ be integers, and let $r$ be an integer with $0 \leq r$ and $\frac{r}{n} \leq 1 - \frac{1}{q}$. Then \[ \Vol_q(r, n) \leq q^{\,n H_q(r/n)}. \]
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
assumptions: $r$ be an integer with $0 \leq r$ and $\frac{r}{n} \leq 1 - \frac{1}{q}$
nodes.statement_short: For $r/n\le 1-1/q$ the Hamming ball volume is at most $q^{nH_q(r/n)}$.
nodes.label: lemma:VolEntropy

nodes.name: Proof of Volume entropy bound
nodes.statement: Write $\lambda = \frac{r}{n}$. If $r = 0$ then $\Vol_q(0, n) = 1 = q^{n H_q(0)}$, so assume $r \geq 1$, giving $0 < \lambda \leq 1 - \frac{1}{q} < 1$. From the definition of $H_q$, \[ q^{n H_q(\lambda)} = (q-1)^{r}\, \lambda^{-r}\,(1-\lambda)^{-(n-r)}, \] so it suffices to show $\Vol_q(r,n)\,(q-1)^{-r}\lambda^{r}(1-\lambda)^{n-r} \leq 1$. Put $\theta = \frac{\lambda}{(q-1)(1-\lambda)}$. Note that $\lambda \leq 1 - \frac{1}{q}$ gives $\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda} \leq q-1$, hence $0 \leq \theta \leq 1$. For each $0 \leq i \leq r$, since $r - i \geq 0$ and $\theta \leq 1$, \[ \binom{n}{i} (q-1)^{i} (q-1)^{-r}\lambda^{r}(1-\lambda)^{n-r} = \binom{n}{i} \lambda^{i} (1-\lambda)^{n-i}\,\theta^{\,r-i} \leq \binom{n}{i} \lambda^{i} (1-\lambda)^{n-i}. \] Summing over $0 \leq i \leq r$ and extending the sum to $0 \leq i \leq n$, \[ \Vol_q(r,n)\,(q-1)^{-r}\lambda^{r}(1-\lambda)^{n-r} \leq \sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i} \lambda^{i}(1-\lambda)^{n-i} = (\lambda + (1-\lambda))^{n} = 1, \] the last step by the binomial theorem. Rearranging gives $\Vol_q(r,n) \leq q^{n H_q(\lambda)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply by $q^{-nH_q(\lambda)}$ and dominate each term by a binomial probability, summing to 1 by the binomial theorem.

nodes.name: Trivial case
nodes.statement: Write $\lambda = \frac{r}{n}$. If $r = 0$ then $\Vol_q(0, n) = 1 = q^{n H_q(0)}$, so assume $r \geq 1$, giving $0 < \lambda \leq 1 - \frac{1}{q} < 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Set $\lambda=r/n$; dispose of $r=0$ and assume $r\ge1$.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: From the definition of $H_q$, \[ q^{n H_q(\lambda)} = (q-1)^{r}\, \lambda^{-r}\,(1-\lambda)^{-(n-r)}, \] so it suffices to show $\Vol_q(r,n)\,(q-1)^{-r}\lambda^{r}(1-\lambda)^{n-r} \leq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $q^{nH_q(\lambda)}$; it suffices to bound a normalized volume by 1.

nodes.name: Define theta
nodes.statement: Put $\theta = \frac{\lambda}{(q-1)(1-\lambda)}$. Note that $\lambda \leq 1 - \frac{1}{q}$ gives $\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda} \leq q-1$, hence $0 \leq \theta \leq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $\theta$ and show $0\le\theta\le1$.

nodes.name: Termwise bound
nodes.statement: For each $0 \leq i \leq r$, since $r - i \geq 0$ and $\theta \leq 1$, \[ \binom{n}{i} (q-1)^{i} (q-1)^{-r}\lambda^{r}(1-\lambda)^{n-r} = \binom{n}{i} \lambda^{i} (1-\lambda)^{n-i}\,\theta^{\,r-i} \leq \binom{n}{i} \lambda^{i} (1-\lambda)^{n-i}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound each term by $\binom{n}{i}\lambda^i(1-\lambda)^{n-i}$.

nodes.name: Binomial theorem
nodes.statement: Summing over $0 \leq i \leq r$ and extending the sum to $0 \leq i \leq n$, \[ \Vol_q(r,n)\,(q-1)^{-r}\lambda^{r}(1-\lambda)^{n-r} \leq \sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i} \lambda^{i}(1-\lambda)^{n-i} = (\lambda + (1-\lambda))^{n} = 1, \] the last step by the binomial theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Sum and extend to $n$; the binomial theorem gives 1.

nodes.name: Rearrange
nodes.statement: Rearranging gives $\Vol_q(r,n) \leq q^{n H_q(\lambda)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Rearrange to the claimed bound.

nodes.name: Linear Code by Subspace
nodes.statement: Let $q$ be a prime power (i.e. $q = p^{s}$ for some prime $p$ and integer $s \geq 1$). $C \subseteq \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$ is a linear code if it is a linear subspace of $\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$. If $C$ has dimenension $k$ and distance $d$ then it will be referred to as an $[n,k,d]_{q}$ or just an $[n,k]_{q}$ code.\footnote{Our lean declaration does not directly depend on code.}
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
differentia: it is a linear subspace of $\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$
nodes.statement_short: A linear code is a subspace of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$; with dimension $k$ and distance $d$ it is an $[n,k,d]_q$ code.
nodes.label: def:LC_subspace

nodes.name: Generator Matrix
nodes.statement: If $C$ is an $[n, k]_{q}$ linear code then there exists a matrix $G \in \mathbb{F}^{k \times n}_{q}$ of rank $k$ satisfying \[C = \{x \cdot G \mid x \in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}.\}\] We define $G$ as a generator matrix of $C$. Note that $G$ is not unique.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
nodes.statement_short: A rank-$k$ matrix $G$ whose row space is the $[n,k]_q$ code $C$.
nodes.label: def:GeneratorMatrix

nodes.name: Parity Check Matrix
nodes.statement: If $C$ is an $[n, k]_{q}$ linear code then there exists a matrix $H \in \mathbb{F}^{(n-k) \times n}_{q}$ of rank $n - k$ satisfying \[C = \{\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q} \mid H \cdot \mathbf{y}^{\intercal} = 0\}.\] We define $H$ as a partiy check matrix of $C$. Note that $H$ is not unique.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
nodes.statement_short: A rank-$(n-k)$ matrix $H$ whose kernel is the $[n,k]_q$ code $C$.
nodes.label: def:ParityCheckMatrix

nodes.name: Subspace Implies Generator
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a linear code that is a $k$-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$. Then there exists a $k \times n$ matrix $G$ with rank $k$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ such that \[ C = \{\mathbf{f}G \mid \mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}\}. \]
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
assumptions: $C$ be a linear code that is a $k$-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$
conclusions: there exists a $k \times n$ matrix $G$ with rank $k$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ such that \[ C = \{\mathbf{f}G \mid \mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}\}. \]
nodes.label: lemma:subspace-imp-generator

nodes.name: Proof of Subspace Implies Generator
nodes.statement: Note that $C$ is a $k$-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$, and thus has a basis $\{\mathbf{g}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{g}_k\}$. Let $G$ be the $k \times n$ matrix whose $i$-th row is $\mathbf{g}_i$. For any $\mathbf{f} = (f_1, \ldots, f_k) \in \mathbb{F}_q^k$, the row-vector product is \[ \mathbf{f}G = \sum_{i=1}^k f_i \mathbf{g}_i. \] Thus $\{\mathbf{f}G \mid f \in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}\}$ is the set of $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear combinations of $\mathbf{g}_{1},\ldots, \mathbf{g}_{k}$. Since $\mathbf{g}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{g}_{k}$ is a basis of $C$ and the span equals $C$, we must have $C = \{\mathbf{f}G \mid f \in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}\}$. It also follows that $rank(G)=k$ since $G$'s rows are basis vectors.
nodes.statement_short: Stack a basis of $C$ as the rows of $G$; the row space is $C$.

nodes.name: Basis
nodes.statement: Note that $C$ is a $k$-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$, and thus has a basis $\{\mathbf{g}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{g}_k\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick a basis of $C$.

nodes.name: Build G
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be the $k \times n$ matrix whose $i$-th row is $\mathbf{g}_i$. For any $\mathbf{f} = (f_1, \ldots, f_k) \in \mathbb{F}_q^k$, the row-vector product is \[ \mathbf{f}G = \sum_{i=1}^k f_i \mathbf{g}_i. \]
nodes.statement_short: Form $G$ from the basis rows; $\mathbf{f}G$ is a linear combination.

nodes.name: Row space
nodes.statement: Thus $\{\mathbf{f}G \mid f \in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}\}$ is the set of $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear combinations of $\mathbf{g}_{1},\ldots, \mathbf{g}_{k}$.
nodes.statement_short: The set $\{\mathbf{f}G\}$ is the span of the basis.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since $\mathbf{g}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{g}_{k}$ is a basis of $C$ and the span equals $C$, we must have $C = \{\mathbf{f}G \mid f \in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}\}$. It also follows that $rank(G)=k$ since $G$'s rows are basis vectors.
nodes.statement_short: Span equals $C$, and rank is $k$.

nodes.name: Generator Implies Subspace
nodes.statement: Let $G \in \mathbb{F}^{k \times n}_{q}$ with rank $k$ and let $C = \{\mathbf{f}G \mid \mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}\}$. Then $C$ is a $k$-dimensional linear code over $\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
nodes.label: lemma:generator-imp-subspace

nodes.name: Proof of Generator Implies Subspace
nodes.statement: First of all, \begin{itemize} \item $\forall \mathbf{c}\in C$, $G$ constrains $\mathbf{c}$ to be $n$ dimensional \item A combination of: \begin{itemize} \item The closure of $\mathbb{F}_q$ under addition and multiplication \item The fact of $\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{f}G$ for some $f\in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}$ \end{itemize} means all elements of $\mathbf{c}$ are in $\mathbb{F}_q$ \end{itemize} This means $\mathbf{c}\in \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$ and therefore $C\subseteq \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$. Given this, it is sufficient to prove $C$ contains the zero vector and is closed under linear addition and scalar multiplication. \begin{itemize} \item We can show that the zero vector $\mathbf{0}\in \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$ is in $C$ because $\mathbf{0}G=\mathbf{0}$. \item We can show that $C$ is closed under addition by considering that $\forall \mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}\in C$, $\exists \mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}$ such that $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{x}G,\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{y}G$, distributivity of matrix multiplication gives us $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{x}G+\mathbf{y}G=(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y})G$, and since $\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}\in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}$ because of closure under addition, $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}=(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y})G\in C $ \item We can show that $C$ is closed under scalar multiplication by considering that $\forall \mathbf{a}\in C$ that $\exists \mathbf{x}\in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}$ such that $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{x}G$. And therefore, $\forall d\in \mathbb{F}_{q}, d\mathbf{a}=d\mathbf{x}G=(d\mathbf{x})G$. And since $d\mathbf{x}\in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}$ by its own closure under scalar multiplication, it must follow $d(\mathbf{x}G)\in C$ These three conditions should be sufficient to prove that $C$ is a valid vector space. \end{itemize} Therefore $C$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$, and because $\{\mathbf{f}G \mid \mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}\}$ is the set of $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear combinations of linearly independent $\mathbf{g}_{1},\ldots, \mathbf{g}_{k}$, it follows that $dim(C)=k$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $C\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q^n$, then verify the subspace axioms; dimension from the independent rows.

nodes.name: Containment
nodes.statement: First of all, \begin{itemize} \item $\forall \mathbf{c}\in C$, $G$ constrains $\mathbf{c}$ to be $n$ dimensional \item A combination of: \begin{itemize} \item The closure of $\mathbb{F}_q$ under addition and multiplication \item The fact of $\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{f}G$ for some $f\in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}$ \end{itemize} means all elements of $\mathbf{c}$ are in $\mathbb{F}_q$ \end{itemize} This means $\mathbf{c}\in \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$ and therefore $C\subseteq \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$.
nodes.statement_short: Codewords lie in $\mathbb{F}_q^n$, so $C\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q^n$.

nodes.name: Length n
nodes.statement: $\forall \mathbf{c}\in C$, $G$ constrains $\mathbf{c}$ to be $n$ dimensional
nodes.statement_short: Codewords have length $n$.

nodes.name: Entries in field
nodes.statement: A combination of: \begin{itemize} \item The closure of $\mathbb{F}_q$ under addition and multiplication \item The fact of $\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{f}G$ for some $f\in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}$ \end{itemize} means all elements of $\mathbf{c}$ are in $\mathbb{F}_q$
nodes.statement_short: Field closure makes entries of $\mathbf{c}$ lie in $\mathbb{F}_q$.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: Given this, it is sufficient to prove $C$ contains the zero vector and is closed under linear addition and scalar multiplication.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to check zero, addition and scalar closure.

nodes.name: Zero vector
nodes.statement: We can show that the zero vector $\mathbf{0}\in \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$ is in $C$ because $\mathbf{0}G=\mathbf{0}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathbf{0}G=\mathbf{0}$.

nodes.name: Additive closure
nodes.statement: We can show that $C$ is closed under addition by considering that $\forall \mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}\in C$, $\exists \mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}$ such that $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{x}G,\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{y}G$, distributivity of matrix multiplication gives us $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{x}G+\mathbf{y}G=(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y})G$, and since $\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}\in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}$ because of closure under addition, $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}=(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y})G\in C $
nodes.statement_short: Distributivity gives closure under addition.

nodes.name: Scalar closure
nodes.statement: We can show that $C$ is closed under scalar multiplication by considering that $\forall \mathbf{a}\in C$ that $\exists \mathbf{x}\in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}$ such that $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{x}G$. And therefore, $\forall d\in \mathbb{F}_{q}, d\mathbf{a}=d\mathbf{x}G=(d\mathbf{x})G$. And since $d\mathbf{x}\in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}$ by its own closure under scalar multiplication, it must follow $d(\mathbf{x}G)\in C$ These three conditions should be sufficient to prove that $C$ is a valid vector space.
nodes.statement_short: Scalars commute with $G$, giving scalar closure.

nodes.name: Dimension
nodes.statement: Therefore $C$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$, and because $\{\mathbf{f}G \mid \mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{F}^{k}_{q}\}$ is the set of $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear combinations of linearly independent $\mathbf{g}_{1},\ldots, \mathbf{g}_{k}$, it follows that $dim(C)=k$.
nodes.statement_short: Subspace with $k$ independent generators, so dimension $k$.

nodes.name: Subspace implies Parity Check
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a linear code that is a $k$-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$. Then there exists a matrix $H \in \mathbb{F}^{(n-k) \times n}_{q}$ with rank $n-k$ such that \[ C = \{\mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q} \mid H\mathbf{f}^{\intercal} = \mathbf{0}\}. \]
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
assumptions: $C$ be a linear code that is a $k$-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$
conclusions: there exists a matrix $H \in \mathbb{F}^{(n-k) \times n}_{q}$ with rank $n-k$ such that \[ C = \{\mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q} \mid H\mathbf{f}^{\intercal} = \mathbf{0}\}. \]
nodes.label: lemma:subspace-imp-parity-check

nodes.name: Proof of Subspace implies Parity Check
nodes.statement: Suppose we take the orthogonal complement of $C$, $C^{\perp}\subseteq \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$. This gives us that \begin{itemize} \item $dim(C^{\perp})=n-dim(C)=n-k$ \item From Lemma~\ref{lemma:subspace-imp-generator}, we know that we can get some $H\in \mathbb{F}^{n-k \times n}_{q}$ such that \[C^{\perp} = \{\mathbf{f}H \mid \mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{F}^{n-k}_{q}\}\] \item And that from Lemma~\ref{lemma:subspace-imp-generator} the rows of $H$ are in $C^{\perp}$ \item From Lemma~\ref{lemma:subspace-imp-generator}, we get generator $G$ for $C$, where $G$'s rows are all basis elements and therefore elements of $C$ \end{itemize} This means that $HG^T$ is the zero matrix since every element is the dot product of some element of $C$ and $C^{\perp}$. This gives us that \[ \forall \mathbf{f}\in \mathbb{F}^k_q, HG^T\mathbf{f}^T = H(\mathbf{f}G)^T = \mathbf{0}\] And by our definition of the generator matrix, \[\forall \mathbf{c} \in C, \exists \mathbf{f}\in \mathbb{F}^k_q, \mathbf{f}G = \mathbf{c}\] \[\implies \forall \mathbf{c} \in C, H\mathbf{c}^T = H(\mathbf{f}G)^T = \mathbf{0}\] \[\implies C \subseteq \{\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q} \mid H\mathbf{c}^{\intercal} = \mathbf{0}\}\] To make notation easier, let's say this subspace (we know it's a subspace because of Lemma~\ref{lemma:parity-check-imp-subspace} below) is $C'=\{\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q} \mid H\mathbf{c}^{\intercal} = \mathbf{0}\}$. We know that \begin{itemize} \item $dim(\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q})=n$ \item $dim(C)=k$ \end{itemize} We can assert that the rank of $H$ is $n-k$ because Lemma~\ref{lemma:subspace-imp-generator} stipulates that $H$ has full rank. From here we can use the rank-nullity theorem to say that, since $C'$ represents the null space of $H$ \[dim(C')+rank(H)=dim(\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q})\] \[\implies dim(C') + n-k = n\] \[\implies dim(C') = k\] and since $dim(C')=dim(C)$ and $C\subseteq C'$, it should follow that $C=C'$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a generator $H$ of $C^\perp$; $C\subseteq\ker H$ and rank-nullity gives equal dimensions.

nodes.name: Dual code
nodes.statement: Suppose we take the orthogonal complement of $C$, $C^{\perp}\subseteq \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$. This gives us that \begin{itemize} \item $dim(C^{\perp})=n-dim(C)=n-k$
nodes.statement_short: Pass to $C^\perp$, of dimension $n-k$.

nodes.name: Generator of dual
nodes.statement: From Lemma~\ref{lemma:subspace-imp-generator}, we know that we can get some $H\in \mathbb{F}^{n-k \times n}_{q}$ such that \[C^{\perp} = \{\mathbf{f}H \mid \mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{F}^{n-k}_{q}\}\]
nodes.statement_short: Get a generator $H$ of $C^\perp$.

nodes.name: Rows in dual
nodes.statement: And that from Lemma~\ref{lemma:subspace-imp-generator} the rows of $H$ are in $C^{\perp}$
nodes.statement_short: Rows of $H$ lie in $C^\perp$.

nodes.name: Generator of C
nodes.statement: From Lemma~\ref{lemma:subspace-imp-generator}, we get generator $G$ for $C$, where $G$'s rows are all basis elements and therefore elements of $C$
nodes.statement_short: Get a generator $G$ of $C$.

nodes.name: Orthogonality
nodes.statement: This means that $HG^T$ is the zero matrix since every element is the dot product of some element of $C$ and $C^{\perp}$. This gives us that \[ \forall \mathbf{f}\in \mathbb{F}^k_q, HG^T\mathbf{f}^T = H(\mathbf{f}G)^T = \mathbf{0}\]
nodes.statement_short: $HG^T=0$, so $H(\mathbf{f}G)^T=0$.

nodes.name: C in kernel
nodes.statement: And by our definition of the generator matrix, \[\forall \mathbf{c} \in C, \exists \mathbf{f}\in \mathbb{F}^k_q, \mathbf{f}G = \mathbf{c}\] \[\implies \forall \mathbf{c} \in C, H\mathbf{c}^T = H(\mathbf{f}G)^T = \mathbf{0}\] \[\implies C \subseteq \{\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q} \mid H\mathbf{c}^{\intercal} = \mathbf{0}\}\]
nodes.statement_short: Every codeword is $\mathbf{f}G$, hence $C\subseteq\ker H$.

nodes.name: Name the kernel
nodes.statement: To make notation easier, let's say this subspace (we know it's a subspace because of Lemma~\ref{lemma:parity-check-imp-subspace} below) is $C'=\{\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q} \mid H\mathbf{c}^{\intercal} = \mathbf{0}\}$. We know that \begin{itemize} \item $dim(\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q})=n$ \item $dim(C)=k$ \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Name the kernel $C'$ and record the dimensions.

nodes.name: Rank-nullity
nodes.statement: We can assert that the rank of $H$ is $n-k$ because Lemma~\ref{lemma:subspace-imp-generator} stipulates that $H$ has full rank. From here we can use the rank-nullity theorem to say that, since $C'$ represents the null space of $H$ \[dim(C')+rank(H)=dim(\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q})\] \[\implies dim(C') + n-k = n\] \[\implies dim(C') = k\] and since $dim(C')=dim(C)$ and $C\subseteq C'$, it should follow that $C=C'$.
nodes.statement_short: Rank-nullity gives $\dim C'=k$, so $C=C'$.

nodes.name: Parity Check Implies subspace
nodes.statement: Let $H \in \mathbb{F}^{(n-k) \times n}_{q}$ with rank $n-k$ and let $C = \{\mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q} \mid H\mathbf{f}^{\intercal} = \mathbf{0}\}$. Then $C$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$ with dimension $k$.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
conclusions: $C$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$ with dimension $k$
nodes.label: lemma:parity-check-imp-subspace

nodes.name: Proof of Parity Check Implies subspace
nodes.statement: Because every $\mathbf{c}\in C$ is defined as being in $\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$, $C \subseteq \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$. It should then be sufficient to prove that $C$ contains the zero vector and is closed under linear addition and scalar multiplication \begin{itemize} \item The zero vector $\mathbf{0}\in \mathbb{F}^{n-k}_{q}$ is in $C$ because $H\mathbf{0}^T=\mathbf{0}$ \item We can show that $C$ is closed under addition by considering that $\forall \mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}\in C, H\mathbf{a}^T=H\mathbf{b}^T=\mathbf{0}$, meaning $H\mathbf{a}^T+H\mathbf{b}^T= \mathbf{0}+\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}$ and therefore by distributivity of matrix multiplication and distributivity of transverses, We have that \[H\mathbf{a}^T+H\mathbf{b}^T = H(\mathbf{a}^T+\mathbf{b}^T) = H(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b})^T = \mathbf{0}\] and since $(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b})\in \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$ by closure of $\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$ under addition, $H(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b})^T = \mathbf{0}$, and $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\in C$ \item We can show that $C$ is closed under scalar multiplication by considering that $\forall \mathbf{a}\in C$ that $H\mathbf{a}^T=0$, then $\forall d\in \mathbb{F}_{q}$, that $H\mathbf{a}^T=\mathbf{0} \implies dH\mathbf{a}^T = d*0=\mathbf{0}$ which $\implies H(d\mathbf{a})^T=\mathbf{0}$ because we can commute scalars with matrices and vectors, giving us that $d\mathbf{a}\in C$ \end{itemize} These three conditions prove that $C$ is a vector space, and is the kernel of $H$. Using rank-nullity theorem, we can see: \[rank(H)+dim(C)=dim(\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q})\] \[\implies n-k+dim(C)=n\] \[\implies dim(C)=k\]
nodes.statement_short: Verify the subspace axioms for $\ker H$, then rank-nullity gives dimension $k$.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: Because every $\mathbf{c}\in C$ is defined as being in $\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$, $C \subseteq \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$. It should then be sufficient to prove that $C$ contains the zero vector and is closed under linear addition and scalar multiplication
nodes.statement_short: $C\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q^n$; suffices to check the subspace axioms.

nodes.name: Zero vector
nodes.statement: The zero vector $\mathbf{0}\in \mathbb{F}^{n-k}_{q}$ is in $C$ because $H\mathbf{0}^T=\mathbf{0}$
nodes.statement_short: $H\mathbf{0}^T=0$.

nodes.name: Additive closure
nodes.statement: We can show that $C$ is closed under addition by considering that $\forall \mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}\in C, H\mathbf{a}^T=H\mathbf{b}^T=\mathbf{0}$, meaning $H\mathbf{a}^T+H\mathbf{b}^T= \mathbf{0}+\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}$ and therefore by distributivity of matrix multiplication and distributivity of transverses, We have that \[H\mathbf{a}^T+H\mathbf{b}^T = H(\mathbf{a}^T+\mathbf{b}^T) = H(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b})^T = \mathbf{0}\] and since $(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b})\in \mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$ by closure of $\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q}$ under addition, $H(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b})^T = \mathbf{0}$, and $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\in C$
nodes.statement_short: Distributivity gives closure under addition.

nodes.name: Scalar closure
nodes.statement: We can show that $C$ is closed under scalar multiplication by considering that $\forall \mathbf{a}\in C$ that $H\mathbf{a}^T=0$, then $\forall d\in \mathbb{F}_{q}$, that $H\mathbf{a}^T=\mathbf{0} \implies dH\mathbf{a}^T = d*0=\mathbf{0}$ which $\implies H(d\mathbf{a})^T=\mathbf{0}$ because we can commute scalars with matrices and vectors, giving us that $d\mathbf{a}\in C$
nodes.statement_short: Scalars commute with $H$, giving scalar closure.

nodes.name: Rank-nullity
nodes.statement: These three conditions prove that $C$ is a vector space, and is the kernel of $H$. Using rank-nullity theorem, we can see: \[rank(H)+dim(C)=dim(\mathbb{F}^{n}_{q})\] \[\implies n-k+dim(C)=n\] \[\implies dim(C)=k\]
nodes.statement_short: Kernel of $H$; rank-nullity gives dimension $k$.

nodes.name: Covering
nodes.statement: Let $q \geq 2$ and $n \geq d \geq 1$ be integers, and let $C \subseteq [q]^{n}$ be a code of minimum distance at least $d$ that is maximal with respect to inclusion. For $\mathbf{c} \in C$, let \[ B(\mathbf{c}, d-1) = \{ \mathbf{z} \in [q]^{n} : \Delta(\mathbf{c}, \mathbf{z}) \le d-1 \} \] denote the Hamming ball of radius $d-1$ centered at $\mathbf{c}$. Then \[ \bigcup_{\mathbf{c} \in C} B(\mathbf{c}, d-1) = [q]^{n}. \]
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
assumptions: $C \subseteq [q]^{n}$ be a code of minimum distance at least $d$ that is maximal with respect to inclusion
nodes.statement_short: Balls of radius $d-1$ around a maximal distance-$d$ code cover $[q]^n$.
nodes.label: lemma:covers

nodes.name: Proof of Covering
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: an uncovered word could be added to $C$, contradicting maximality.

nodes.name: Uncovered word
nodes.statement_short: An uncovered $\mathbf{z}$ could be added to $C$, contradicting maximality.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence every $\mathbf{z}$ lies in $B(c,d-1)$ and \[[q]^{n} = \bigcup_{\mathbf{c} \in C} B(\mathbf{c},d-1).\]
nodes.statement_short: Every word is covered.

nodes.name: Maximal Packing
nodes.statement: Let $q \geq 2$ and $n \geq d \geq 1$ be integers, and let $C \subseteq [q]^n$ be maximal, with respect to inclusion, among all codes of minimum distance at least $d$. Then \[ |C| \geq \frac{q^n}{\Vol_q(n,d-1)}. \]
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); conventions of Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
assumptions: $C \subseteq [q]^n$ be maximal, with respect to inclusion, among all codes of minimum distance at least $d$
nodes.statement_short: A maximal code of distance $d$ has at least $q^n/\Vol_q(n,d-1)$ codewords.
nodes.label: lemma:MaximalPacking

nodes.name: Proof of Maximal Packing
nodes.statement: For every codeword $c \in C$ we define a ball $B(\mathbf{c},d-1)$. Note that by Lemma~\ref{lemma:covers}, the union of these balls cover $[q]^{n}$. Then we must have the following inequality, \[ q^{n} = |[q]^{n}| = \left|\bigcup_{\mathbf{c} \in C}B(\mathbf{c}, d-1)\right| \leq \sum_{\mathbf{c} \in C} |B(\mathbf{c},d-1)| = |C| \cdot \Vol_{q}(n,d-1) \implies |C| \geq \frac{q^{n}}{\Vol_{q}(n,d-1)}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Union bound over the covering balls of Lemma Covering.

nodes.name: Covering balls
nodes.statement: For every codeword $c \in C$ we define a ball $B(\mathbf{c},d-1)$. Note that by Lemma~\ref{lemma:covers}, the union of these balls cover $[q]^{n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Balls around codewords cover $[q]^n$ by Lemma Covering.

nodes.name: Union bound
nodes.statement: Then we must have the following inequality, \[ q^{n} = |[q]^{n}| = \left|\bigcup_{\mathbf{c} \in C}B(\mathbf{c}, d-1)\right| \leq \sum_{\mathbf{c} \in C} |B(\mathbf{c},d-1)| = |C| \cdot \Vol_{q}(n,d-1) \implies |C| \geq \frac{q^{n}}{\Vol_{q}(n,d-1)}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Union bound yields $|C|\ge q^n/\Vol_q(n,d-1)$.

nodes.name: Gilbert-Varshamov Bound; general codes
nodes.statement: See~\cite{GRS}. Let $q \geq 2$ be an integer. For every $0 \leq \delta < 1 - \frac{1}{q}$ and every positive integer $n$, there exists a $q$-ary code of block length $n$ with rate $R \geq 1 - H_q(\delta)$ and relative distance at least $\delta$.
nodes.origin_citation: Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
conclusions: there exists a $q$-ary code of block length $n$ with rate $R \geq 1 - H_q(\delta)$ and relative distance at least $\delta$
nodes.statement_short: Codes of rate $\ge 1-H_q(\delta)$ and relative distance $\ge\delta$ exist for $\delta<1-1/q$.
nodes.label: thm:GVBgc

nodes.name: Proof of Gilbert-Varshamov Bound; general codes
nodes.statement: Fix $\delta$ with $0 \leq \delta < 1 - \frac{1}{q}$ and a positive integer $n$, and put \[ d = \max(\lceil \delta n \rceil, 1). \] Then $d \geq 1$, and $d \leq n$ since $\delta < 1$ gives $\lceil \delta n \rceil \leq n$, so $n \geq d \geq 1$. Note also $d \geq \delta n$ and $d - 1 \leq \delta n$. The codes $C \subseteq [q]^{n}$ of minimum distance at least $d$ form a finite nonempty family (any singleton works), so we may pick one, call it $C$, that is maximal with respect to inclusion. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:MaximalPacking}, \[ |C| \geq \frac{q^{n}}{\Vol_{q}(n,d-1)}. \] Since $\Vol_{q}(n,d-1) \leq q^{n}$ we have $|C| \geq 1$, so taking $\log_{q}$ and dividing by $n$, \[ R = \frac{\log_{q}|C|}{n} \geq 1 - \frac{\log_{q}\Vol_{q}(d-1,n)}{n}. \] Note that $0 \leq \frac{d-1}{n} \leq \delta < 1 - \frac{1}{q}$, so by Lemma~\ref{lemma:VolEntropy} at $\lambda = \frac{d-1}{n}$, \[ \Vol_{q}(n,d-1) \leq q^{\,n H_q(\frac{d-1}{n})} \implies \frac{\log_{q}\Vol_{q}(d-1,n)}{n} \leq H_q\!\left(\tfrac{d-1}{n}\right), \] and hence $R \geq 1 - H_q(\frac{d-1}{n})$. Finally $H_q$ is nondecreasing on $[0, 1 - \frac{1}{q}]$ by the monotonicity of $H_q$ and $\frac{d-1}{n} \leq \delta$, so $H_q(\frac{d-1}{n}) \leq H_q(\delta)$ and \[ R \geq 1 - H_q(\delta). \] The relative distance of $C$ is at least $\frac{d}{n} \geq \delta$. Hence $C$ is a $q$-ary code of block length $n$ with rate $R \geq 1 - H_q(\delta)$ and relative distance at least $\delta$ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Greedy/maximal code argument: Maximal Packing bounds $|C|$, then the volume entropy bound and monotonicity of $H_q$ give the rate.

nodes.name: Choose d
nodes.statement: Fix $\delta$ with $0 \leq \delta < 1 - \frac{1}{q}$ and a positive integer $n$, and put \[ d = \max(\lceil \delta n \rceil, 1). \] Then $d \geq 1$, and $d \leq n$ since $\delta < 1$ gives $\lceil \delta n \rceil \leq n$, so $n \geq d \geq 1$. Note also $d \geq \delta n$ and $d - 1 \leq \delta n$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $\delta,n$ and set $d=\max(\lceil\delta n\rceil,1)$.

nodes.name: Maximal code
nodes.statement: The codes $C \subseteq [q]^{n}$ of minimum distance at least $d$ form a finite nonempty family (any singleton works), so we may pick one, call it $C$, that is maximal with respect to inclusion.
nodes.statement_short: Pick a maximal code of minimum distance at least $d$.

nodes.name: Apply Maximal Packing
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lemma:MaximalPacking}, \[ |C| \geq \frac{q^{n}}{\Vol_{q}(n,d-1)}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Lower-bound $|C|$ by Maximal Packing.

nodes.name: Take logs
nodes.statement: Since $\Vol_{q}(n,d-1) \leq q^{n}$ we have $|C| \geq 1$, so taking $\log_{q}$ and dividing by $n$, \[ R = \frac{\log_{q}|C|}{n} \geq 1 - \frac{\log_{q}\Vol_{q}(d-1,n)}{n}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Take $\log_q$ and divide by $n$ to bound $R$.

nodes.name: Apply entropy bound
nodes.statement: Note that $0 \leq \frac{d-1}{n} \leq \delta < 1 - \frac{1}{q}$, so by Lemma~\ref{lemma:VolEntropy} at $\lambda = \frac{d-1}{n}$, \[ \Vol_{q}(n,d-1) \leq q^{\,n H_q(\frac{d-1}{n})} \implies \frac{\log_{q}\Vol_{q}(d-1,n)}{n} \leq H_q\!\left(\tfrac{d-1}{n}\right), \] and hence $R \geq 1 - H_q(\frac{d-1}{n})$.
nodes.statement_short: Volume entropy bound gives $R\ge1-H_q((d-1)/n)$.

nodes.name: Monotonicity
nodes.statement: Finally $H_q$ is nondecreasing on $[0, 1 - \frac{1}{q}]$ by the monotonicity of $H_q$ and $\frac{d-1}{n} \leq \delta$, so $H_q(\frac{d-1}{n}) \leq H_q(\delta)$ and \[ R \geq 1 - H_q(\delta). \]
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity of $H_q$ gives $R\ge1-H_q(\delta)$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: The relative distance of $C$ is at least $\frac{d}{n} \geq \delta$. Hence $C$ is a $q$-ary code of block length $n$ with rate $R \geq 1 - H_q(\delta)$ and relative distance at least $\delta$ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Relative distance at least $\delta$; done.

nodes.name: Gilbert-Varshamov Bound; linear codes
nodes.statement: See~\cite{GRS}. Let $q$ be a prime power. For every $0 \leq \delta < 1 - \frac{1}{q}$, every $0 \leq \varepsilon \leq 1 - H_q(\delta)$, and every positive integer $n$, set $k = n\bigl(1 - H_q(\delta) - \varepsilon\bigr)$. If $G \in \mathbb{F}^{k \times n}_{q}$ is picked uniformly at random, then $G$ generates a code of rate $1 - H_q(\delta) - \varepsilon$ and relative distance at least $\delta$ with probability strictly greater than $1 - q^{-\varepsilon n}$.
nodes.origin_citation: Guruswami, Rudra, Sudan, Essential Coding Theory (GRS)
assumptions: $G \in \mathbb{F}^{k \times n}_{q}$ is picked uniformly at random
conclusions: $G$ generates a code of rate $1 - H_q(\delta) - \varepsilon$ and relative distance at least $\delta$ with probability strictly greater than $1 - q^{-\varepsilon n}$
nodes.statement_short: A uniformly random generator matrix gives a linear code beating the GV rate minus $\varepsilon$ w.h.p.
